Commerce Department investigators examining whether Nvidia chips bought by Megaspeed reached China were told in 2025 to clear all contact with Nvidia through a political appointee, weeks after Nvidia's top lawyer telephoned him.
The Commerce Department has not identified the official who issued that instruction or the authority under which it was issued. Nor has it said whether the instruction, or a separate order not to name Megaspeed in external communications, affected an investigation that the Justice Department later asked the bureau to pause and then took over.
Jeffrey Kessler, the under secretary for industry and security, runs the Bureau of Industry and Security, the Commerce Department agency that enforces export controls, and reports directly to Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary. Kessler did not respond to questions from reporters about the instruction. "BIS conducts all enforcement strictly by the book," a bureau spokesman said, adding that enforcement was at an all-time high.
Tim Teter, Nvidia's general counsel, called Kessler before the instruction was issued, and in August 2025 he emailed the agents on the case to say Kessler had allowed Nvidia to contact them. The order of events does not show that the call prompted the instruction or that the instruction changed any investigative decision. A Commerce official said Kessler told the agents to handle the case by the book and did not direct them to share information with Nvidia.
Nvidia said Teter contacted the department to provide information, understand regulatory requirements and help stop illegal transshipment. John Rizzo, who runs public policy communications at Nvidia, said the company consulted officials to answer their questions. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing and has not been charged. The Justice Department, which now runs a criminal inquiry into the company, declined to comment on a continuing investigation.
The case the agents were building
Megaspeed International, a Singapore data centre company, bought at least US$4.8 billion of equipment containing Nvidia technology between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records. Nvidia reported data centre revenue of US$51.2 billion in the quarter to 26 October 2025, so that total equals about 9 per cent of one quarter's data centre sales.
Shipping Nvidia chips to a company in Malaysia or Indonesia that is not owned from China is generally lawful without a licence, and renting their computing power to Chinese customers over the internet is in most cases not controlled. Moving the chips into China without a licence, or buying them on behalf of a Chinese company, is prohibited. The bureau's agents were examining whether some of Megaspeed's equipment had crossed that line.
An official from the bureau visited Megaspeed's Malaysian data centre in September 2024 and found Nvidia equipment still packed in boxes. Megaspeed had imported tens of thousands more chips than Nvidia counted when it checked the company's data centres, and two of the eight operators Nvidia told U.S. officials it had visited said they held no Megaspeed hardware. Megaspeed said on 23 December 2025 that the bureau, Malaysia's trade ministry and Nvidia had all inspected it and found no illegal diversion.
Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman also known as Huang Le, became Megaspeed's controlling shareholder in March 2023, according to C4ADS, a Washington research group. The shares passed in late 2023 to Swiftdata, a Singapore company whose ultimate owner C4ADS could not identify. Singapore police questioned Alice Huang in 2025 over false import declarations and barred her from leaving the country. People briefed on classified surveillance have said U.S. officials concluded in 2025 that she was passing information to the Chinese government.
Teter's call and the instruction
Teter telephoned Kessler in late summer 2025 and asked about the Megaspeed investigation. He asked in particular whether the bureau had played any part when Singapore police questioned Alice Huang, and people familiar with the matter said it had not. Whether Teter made any specific request about the bureau's own investigation is not known. Nvidia said Teter did not know of Jensen Huang's affair with Alice Huang when he made the call.
In the weeks that followed, bureau staff were told to route all requests involving Nvidia through Kessler or obtain his approval before contacting the company. They were also told not to mention Megaspeed or its Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix, in external communications. People familiar with the instructions called the first unusual and said it applied only to Nvidia.
No published account names the official who issued either instruction, gives its date or says whether it was put in writing. None says whether Lutnick approved it. Kessler and the Commerce Department have not addressed those points in public.
Kessler and other department leaders had already required, since Trump's return to office, that any investigation of Nvidia and any outreach to the company first receive their approval. Jensen Huang has been an influential voice on export policy with Trump and Lutnick, and Nvidia has argued against export controls.
The August email
The bureau's agents had been examining Megaspeed for months when Teter wrote to them in August 2025. He asked for information about the inquiry and requested a meeting with one of the agents, who declined. Teter replied that he did not understand the refusal, because Kessler had said Nvidia could communicate with the bureau's staff, according to people familiar with the exchange.
Agents were alarmed that the email invoked Kessler, their superior and a Trump nominee. They forwarded the chain to him, and Kessler replied within hours that they should keep handling the case strictly by the book, a Commerce official said. The official said Kessler had not directed staff to share information with Nvidia or advised them which meetings to take.
Kessler's reply is the only instruction from him on the case described in published accounts. Whether he had in fact told Teter that Nvidia could contact the agents, and on what terms, has not been disclosed.
Authority over the investigators
The bureau's enforcement agents work in its export enforcement office, led by an assistant secretary who reports to the under secretary. David Peters held that post in March 2026, when he told Congress that chip smuggling was among the office's top enforcement priorities. Peters has not commented publicly on the Nvidia instruction.
A temporary denial order, the bureau's quickest administrative tool against a company suspected of an imminent violation, cuts off its export privileges for up to 180 days without a hearing. The assistant secretary for export enforcement issues such orders at the request of the enforcement office. A company can appeal to an administrative law judge, whose recommendation goes to the under secretary for a decision.
Kessler, who would rule on any such appeal, would normally be walled off from the details of an investigation so that he could act as a neutral arbiter in any eventual enforcement decision, Commerce officials said. His dealings with Nvidia could be subject to legal discovery or a subpoena if an enforcement case goes ahead.
The Commerce Department does not publish the internal rules that govern contact between its enforcement agents, political appointees and companies under investigation, and the bureau's enforcement manuals are not public. The Justice Department has a written policy. Its manual and an attorney general's memorandum of 21 July 2021 restrict communications with the White House about pending investigations to a small number of named officials, to insulate prosecutors from inappropriate influence. Neither governs Commerce Department officials or contact from companies.
Why officials objected
Some Commerce officials regarded Kessler's dealings with Nvidia as a breach of government procedure that could taint the case. They questioned why the department was discussing the matter with a company that had not been ruled out as a subject of the investigation. Megaspeed was Nvidia's largest Southeast Asian buyer and an official Nvidia Cloud Partner, a status Nvidia granted four days after the late-2023 change in ownership.
Commerce officials convened meetings about Teter's email and disclosed it to partner law enforcement agencies. Officials who described the episode have not said that Kessler ordered agents to stop work, and the Justice Department's criminal inquiry means the case has not been dropped.
The pause and the transfer
The Justice Department, which had been working on the case with the bureau, asked it to pause its work in late 2025, and the Commerce Department complied, one person familiar with the case said. The case was later transferred to the Justice Department. In one account the request came after Commerce officials told partner agencies about Teter's contact.
Export cases are often pursued jointly by the two departments, and the Justice Department can take the lead where a case involves criminality or intelligence. A pause of the bureau's work is standard when its investigation becomes a criminal one. The transfer was unusual because the agents had spent months on the case and could have pursued administrative action to restrict Megaspeed's access to U.S. technology.
No Justice Department official has said why the department asked for the pause or whether Teter's contact played any part. It has not said whether it has examined the August 2025 contacts.
The effect on enforcement
Agents who had spent months building the case were frustrated, and the halt may have delayed action to stop shipments to Megaspeed. People familiar with the case said the bureau had made no progress after the pause, although they regarded the evidence as sufficient to proceed.
Nvidia halted all sales and shipments to Megaspeed in June 2025, a company spokesman said, though the Commerce Department has since permitted parts and replacement components. Malaysian trade records show Megaspeed imported at least 17,544 Nvidia GB300 chips, worth about US$787 million, in November 2025. The records do not show whether they came from Nvidia's hardware partners before the halt, from distributors or by some other route.
U.S. agencies outside the Commerce Department have proposed adding Megaspeed to the Entity List, the department's trade blacklist, and the department has not done so. Additions are decided by majority vote of an interagency committee that the Commerce Department chairs, according to the department's rules. Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas, a Republican, urged Lutnick on 13 October 2025 to investigate the company. The department has added no company to the list since 9 October 2025, when it published its last additions, and the freeze applies across the whole list.
Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary, pressed Lutnick at a White House meeting on 5 November on why Megaspeed had not been listed, people familiar with the exchange said. Kessler, warned about the company in deputies' meetings, had deferred to Lutnick on the decision. Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said the two secretaries had no such conversation.
Gregory Meeks, the senior Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a Democratic representative from California, had raised a wider halt in February 2026. They asked Lutnick whether the department had shelved other China-related security actions, including proposed bans on Chinese telecoms and router businesses, to steady relations with China.
Questions to Commerce and Nvidia
About three months before Teter's Commerce contacts became public, he told a White House official that Alice Huang was "not as important" in Megaspeed as she had made out, according to a person familiar with the call. He said Nvidia had stopped doing business with Megaspeed because of bad publicity.
Nvidia has given no account of Teter's contacts beyond its statement of 9 November. Its independent directors retained Joon H. Kim, a former acting U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, on 10 November to run the investigation the board announced two days earlier. The board has not said whether that inquiry will cover Nvidia's dealings with the Commerce Department.
Three Republican House committee chairs have asked Jensen Huang to brief them in closed session on 18 November. Brian Mast, who chairs the Foreign Affairs Committee, said on 10 November that he was prepared to subpoena Jensen Huang if he did not respond. John Moolenaar, the House China committee chairman, said on 11 November that a subpoena was likely if he did not agree that day.
Meeks, Kamlager-Dove and Gabe Amo, a Democratic representative from Rhode Island, asked Lutnick on 9 November to explain what his officials knew about Megaspeed and why export approvals continued. They asked for written answers by 1 December.

I spent the day analyzing $RIOT's Corsicana lease with a Frontier AI Lab, and what a similar deal could mean for $NUAI.

Here are the facts on Corsicana:

- 910 critical IT MW on 1 GW gross. $130/kW-mo, escalating 3%/yr, billed on the full 910 MW whether used or not. Tenant can flex usage seasonally within the 1 GW load.

- $28B over the 15-year initial term ($54B with extensions). ~33% average unlevered yield on cost (!!)

- Capex: ~$2M/MW for the HV/MV power pad (~$1.8B), plus up to $4M/MW reimbursed to the tenant for modules (~$3.6B), paid per phase only after modules are delivered.

- Delivery: 400 MW Sep 2027, 200 MW Jan 2028, 310 MW Jul 2028. Rent starts no later than 60 days after each block is delivered.

- Equipment: first 400 MW substation is operating. No backup generation, so no air permits needed.

- Financing: base case is 80-90% LTC non-recourse project debt ($4.4 to 4.9B) on tenant credit. I believe they will have negotiated a fallback strategy if financing doesn't come to fruition.

This deal is a paradigm shift and the new gold standard for every datacenter developed out there.

Here's my read-through to $NUAI (my napkin math):

- TCDC in Ector County has 207 MW of Luminant power come Q3 2027 (Vistra gets 5% of the Phase 1 project company) and ~500 MW more planned on behind-the-meter gas.

- On the Riot structure at ~690 IT MW and $125/kW-mo: ~$19B of contract value, ~$1.3B average NOI, ~31% unlevered yield on cost. Tenant funds the modules, project debt funds most of the pad, and the equity check is under $100M.

- At a 10x NOI, with a 40% haircut on Phase 2 for the air permit, turbines and timing, I get ~$27/share in a base case, against ~$2 today, with ~10% dilution at current prices. That's $11/sh on Phase 1 alone.

Of course, it all hinges on what mgmt can deliver. NUAI still has to sign a tenant and Phase 2 needs an air permit that Texas won't process until the ERCOT audit wraps December 10th. 

Q3 results and call on tap tomorrow at 8am ET.

Looking forward to it!

The fall of “what you can do” and the rise of “who you know”

Traditionally, many of us believe in a world where how hard you work is more important than who you know. I used to subscribe to this idea as both a scientist, who believed that facts about our world are agnostic to who says them, and as an American, who grew up believing that success was a function of how hard you worked, not who you knew.

However I am now feeling a substantial change in AI, specifically in the past five years, where who you know is becoming more important, and what you can do is becoming less important. I am obviously not saying that technical skills don’t matter, or that you cannot be successful without being well connected. Technical skills are still important and make or break your career. But I am noticing a trend. To assign arbitrary numbers, I would say that five years ago, success was 75% your skills and 25% who you knew. Now, it is maybe 55% skills and 45% who you know.

There are three technical reasons for this trend. The first is the commoditization of intelligence—coding agents have basically democratized research execution. In the past you could outwork competitors by staying up late to debug code or babysitting your experiments with higher frequency. Now, many research tasks can be completed by anyone who knows what to prompt. Research taste obviously still matters, but the playing field is definitely more equal. As technical execution becomes less of a differentiator, other advantages naturally become more important.

The second reason for this trend is that with the success of scaling language models, it is simply a fact that being resource rich makes you so much more likely to succeed. Ten years ago, an academic lab with eight GPUs had a real chance of doing great research. Now, a single RL run can require hundreds (if not thousands) of GPUs, as well as substantial data and infra. So now, two equally capable researchers can have very different outcomes depending what resources they have. And access to these resources is not a function of technical skill alone. It also depends on reputation, trust built with decision-makers, and professional relationships. These things have always mattered, but as the resource requirements of frontier AI have grown, so too has their importance.

Third, when companies stopped publishing research and moved to secretive, closed-source models, AI became a field of poor observability. In domains of perfect observability like chess or soccer, it is very easy to tell who is doing well and understand their contributions. But now in AI we have fewer public mechanisms for attributing credit, making it much harder for outsiders to know who did what for model launches. How does this get resolved? When it's difficult to independently verify someone's technical contributions, people increasingly rely on indirect signals such as reputation, personal endorsements, and who will vouch for them. Consequently, who you know plays a much bigger role in hiring, recruiting, and fundraising.

We often talk about how to improve technical skills, but nobody really talks about how to get better at "who you know". One observation is that many well-connected people mix their work and personal lives. The traditional wisdom is to keep a firm boundary between the two, which in the past was a very reasonable policy. But the returns of being social have gone up, which means that anyone still holding to that boundary is paying a much steeper price for it than they would have before.

Sam Altman is the prime example of a well-connected person who mixes work and personal. There is so much to learn from Sam. For example, back when OpenAI was smaller, Sam invited almost all the employees to his house for social hours. He hosts poker nights and dinners at his house for recruiting purposes. Sam has a reputation of being generous with his time and treating his friends well and I think that has yielded a disproportionate return for him. Obviously not all interpersonal relationships at OpenAI went perfectly but I think a large part of OpenAI’s success is from Sam’s connections.

The interesting thing about this is that intentionally trying hard at getting to know people is probably the suboptimal strategy. I don't think Sam made his connections because he knew they would pay off in his career, but rather because he is a generous person who is innately curious about people and technology. Perhaps the best strategy is to be your best and truest self, which is easier said than done, especially in a changing technological world.

While these technical trends have made the field less dependent on technical merit, I don’t think this is necessarily a bad thing, and it is not the first time this has happened in our field. For example, abstractions introduced by Python also made coding less technical and enabled more people to code. And with some skillsets, there is more opportunity now than ever. For instance, people without programming backgrounds can now create great technology, with product or research taste as more salient levers. So while what we can do is commoditized, what we choose to do, and who we do it with will matter more than ever.

Thanks Edward Hu for feedback on this essay.

MY HUSBAND'S BEST FRIEND ASKED ME TO HAVE A BABY WITH HIM

My husband and I had been married for six years, but we had one problem: we couldn't have children.

We had visited several hospitals, tried different treatments and even travelled to another state for medical consultations.

Unfortunately, nothing worked.

My husband, Daniel, was always supportive. He constantly reminded me that we could still have a happy marriage without children.

But his mother wasn't as understanding.

Whenever she visited, she made comments about grandchildren and how badly she wanted to carry one before she died.

One evening, Daniel's best friend, Marcus, came over for dinner.

Marcus had been part of our lives for years. He was practically family, and I had never seen him as anything more than my husband's closest friend.

During dinner, the conversation somehow turned to our fertility problems.

Marcus looked at Daniel and said:

"Have you guys considered using a donor?"

Daniel laughed and replied:

"We've discussed everything already. We're tired of trying."

I didn't think much of the conversation until Marcus started visiting more frequently.

One afternoon, while Daniel was at work, Marcus came over unexpectedly.

We were talking when he suddenly said:

"There's something I've wanted to discuss with you, but I don't know how you'll take it."

I asked what it was.

He looked uncomfortable before finally saying:

"I know this sounds crazy, but what if I helped you have a baby?"

I stared at him.

"How exactly do you mean?"

He took a deep breath.

"I mean, I could be the biological father. Daniel wouldn't have to know."

I immediately stood up and told him to leave.

But before he walked out, he said something that made me question everything.

"Ask Daniel why he has refused every fertility test I've suggested he take."
